q.q: What is the full title of the consumer law that protects people buying online, by phone or by post?
o: Consumer Contracts (Information, Delivery and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013
Consumer Rights (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2015
Distance Selling (Information, Cancellation and Hidden Charges) Regulations 2013
Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013
q.why: The full title is the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013; examiners have asked for it word for word.

q.q: What is a distance contract?
o: A contract signed in a shop for goods that will be delivered a long way away
A licence that lets software be used on computers at more than one site
An agreement between a shop and a delivery company to carry its parcels
A purchase made online, by phone or by catalogue where the buyer cannot see the goods first
q.why: Buying online, by phone or from a catalogue without seeing, touching or trying the product is a distance contract.

q.q: Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, when does the 14-day cooling-off period for goods begin?
o: The day the order is placed
The day after the goods arrive
The day payment is taken
Seven days after delivery
q.why: For goods, the 14 days start on the day after the goods arrive. For a service they start the day after the contract is agreed.

q.q: A pair of headphones bought online is delivered on 3 March. Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013, what is the last day the buyer can cancel for a change of mind?
o: 16 March
18 March
17 March
14 March
q.why: The 14 days start the day after delivery (4 March), so day 14 is 17 March. 16 March wrongly counts delivery day as day 1.

q.q: Which of these can normally be returned for a change of mind within 14 days?
o: A hoodie printed with the buyer's name
A game disc whose seal has been broken
A film download that has been started
Unworn trainers still in their box
q.why: Ordinary unused goods can be returned. Personalised items, unsealed discs and started downloads are exceptions.

q.q: A shopping website adds '£3.99 priority handling' to every order with the box already ticked. Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 this is...
o: allowed, as long as the customer is able to untick the box
allowed, as long as the price of the extra is shown clearly
only banned when the order is for digital content
banned, because extra payments need the customer to actively opt in
q.why: Pre-ticked boxes that add an extra payment are banned; the customer must actively opt in.

q.q: A customer cancels an online order and posts the goods back. Within what time must the trader refund her?
o: 30 days of the date the order was first placed
7 days of the customer phoning to cancel the order
28 days of the goods first being delivered
14 days of getting the goods back or of proof of posting
q.why: The trader must refund, including standard delivery, within 14 days of getting the goods back or of the customer showing proof of posting.

q.q: Before a customer pays, which information must a trader give under the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013?
o: The total price including VAT and delivery, and the right to cancel
The trader's profit on the item and where it was manufactured
The names of other customers who have bought the same item
The customer's credit score and how it affects the price
q.why: Traders must give their identity and contact details, the main features, the total price including VAT and delivery, and the right to cancel.

q.q: When does copyright protection begin for a new original work in the UK?
o: Only when the work has been registered with the government
Only when the © symbol has been added to the work
Only when the work has been sold for the first time
Automatically, as soon as the work is recorded or saved
q.why: Copyright is automatic as soon as an original work is recorded or saved; no form or © symbol is needed.

q.q: How does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 treat a computer program?
o: As a design, so it is only protected once it has been registered
As a service, so it is protected for only 14 days after sale
As data, so it is protected by data protection law instead
As a literary work, so its source code is protected like a novel
q.why: The Act treats a computer program as a literary work, so its source code is protected in the same way as a novel.

q.q: A software author died in 2000. Using the normal rule for software, until when does copyright in her program last?
o: 2050, her life plus 50 years
2070, her life plus 70 years
2000, the year that she died
2088, 100 years after the Act
q.why: For software, music, books and images, copyright normally lasts for the creator's life plus 70 years: 2000 + 70 = 2070.

q.q: A programmer writes an app as part of her job at a software company. Who normally owns the copyright?
o: The employer
The programmer
The app store
The first customer
q.why: Work produced as part of a job normally belongs to the employer.

q.q: A school 'buys' a graphics package. What has it actually bought?
o: The copyright in the software and its code
A licence to use the software on agreed terms
The source code, so it can change the program
The right to sell copies to other schools
q.why: Buying software means buying a licence; the developer keeps the copyright.

q.q: Which statement about freeware is correct?
o: It is not protected by any copyright law at all
It always allows its source code to be changed
It can be sold by anyone who downloads it
It is free to use but still owned by its developer
q.why: Free software is not automatically copyright-free: freeware is still owned by its developer.

q.q: Which is a sensible step for an organisation to stay within the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988?
o: Keep a record of which licences are owned and who uses them
Let every member of staff install any program they need
Remove the © symbol from all documents it produces
Store all software on the cloud so licences are not needed
q.why: A sensible policy: inform staff, let only the IT team install programs, keep licence records and block unauthorised downloads.

q.q: What is the maximum prison sentence for serious commercial or online copyright infringement?
o: Up to 2 years
Up to 10 years
Up to 6 months
Up to life
q.why: Breaking the Act can lead to unlimited fines and, for serious commercial or online infringement, up to 10 years in prison.

q.q: What is software piracy?
o: Breaking the terms of a genuine licence that the user has paid for
Illegally copying, downloading, distributing or selling software without permission
Gaining access to a computer system without the owner's permission
Copying an essay from a website and handing it in as your own
q.why: Software piracy is illegally copying, downloading, distributing or selling software without the owner's permission. Breaking the terms of a genuine licence is a licensing infringement.

q.q: A company buys a single-user licence and installs the program on 12 office PCs. This is...
o: allowed, as long as the 12 PCs are all connected to one network
an offence under section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990
a licensing infringement under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
allowed, because the company did pay for a genuine licence
q.why: Installing beyond the number allowed breaks the licence terms, which breaches copyright law.

q.q: A school has a network licence for 30 users, but 45 pupils need to use the software at the same time. How many more user licences does it need to stay legal?
q.why: 45 users minus the 30 already licensed = 15 more user licences.

q.q: A firm with a site licence for its Belfast office also installs the software at its new branch in Lisburn. Why is this a breach?
o: A site licence only covers a single user at a time
A site licence ends when a new branch is opened
A site licence covers computers at one location only
A site licence only allows use for home learning
q.why: A site licence allows any number of computers at one location; installing at a second branch breaks its terms.

q.q: A student uses software bought on a cheap education licence to run a paid design business. What is the breach?
o: Installing the software on too many computers
Selling copies of the software at a market
Using the licence for a purpose it does not allow
Sharing the licence key with friends online
q.why: Education and home licences allow learning or personal use only; using one to run a business breaks the licence terms.

q.q: Which of these is software piracy?
o: Selling copied games at a car-boot sale
Buying a site licence for a school
Using open source code within its licence
Updating anti-virus software
q.why: Copying and selling software without permission is piracy.

q.q: A pupil copies an essay from a website and submits it as their own work. What is this mainly?
o: Plagiarism
Software piracy
Phishing
Unauthorised access
q.why: Plagiarism is copying someone else's work and handing it in as your own; it may also infringe copyright if the material is protected.

q.q: A pupil logs into a teacher's account with a guessed password but changes nothing. Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 this is...
o: unauthorised access, an offence under section 1
legal, because no data was changed or deleted
only an offence if the data is later deleted
an offence under section 3 for impairing a computer
q.why: Section 1 is committed by access without permission, whether or not anything is changed.

q.q: A hacker breaks into an online shop's database to steal card numbers for fraud. Which section best fits this access?
o: Section 1 only
Section 3A
Section 2
Section 3ZA
q.why: Unauthorised access with intent to commit a further offence, such as fraud, is section 2.

q.q: Which act is an offence under section 3 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
o: Changing someone's password to lock them out of their account
Logging in to a classmate's account just to look at their files
Selling password-cracking tools to other criminals online
Attacking a hospital's systems so that lives are put at risk
q.why: Section 3 covers unauthorised acts intended to impair a computer, such as changing passwords, deleting files or planting a virus. Selling tools is 3A and serious damage is 3ZA.

q.q: Someone sells ransomware kits online. Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers this?
o: Section 1
Section 2
Section 3A
Section 3ZA
q.why: Section 3A covers making, supplying or obtaining tools to commit Computer Misuse Act offences.

q.q: A hacker logs into a company network without permission and then deletes its customer records. How many offences have been committed?
o: One: section 3, because only deletion is a crime
Two: section 1 for the access and section 3 for deleting
One: section 1, because only access is a crime
None, unless the records contained personal data
q.why: One act can break several sections: logging in (s1), then deleting records (s3).

q.q: What is the key test for whether an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 has been committed?
o: Was any data actually stolen?
Was the computer damaged?
Was money made from the act?
Did the person have permission?
q.why: Permission is everything: section 1 is committed even if nothing is changed or taken.

q.q: Which statement correctly separates the Computer Misuse Act 1990 from data protection law?
o: The Computer Misuse Act covers how organisations handle personal data; data protection law covers hacking
The Computer Misuse Act covers copying software; data protection law covers unauthorised access to computers
The Computer Misuse Act covers unauthorised access to computers; data protection law covers how organisations handle personal data
The Computer Misuse Act covers online shopping; data protection law covers deleting files on a computer
q.why: The Computer Misuse Act is about unauthorised access to and interference with computers; data protection law is about handling personal data.

q.q: Which best describes a hacker?
o: Malware that attaches itself to files and copies itself into others
A person who gets into a computer system or its data without permission
Malware that secretly records a user's activity and sends it on
A person paid to install software on an organisation's computers
q.why: A hacker is a person who gets into a computer system without permission. The other descriptions are a virus and spyware.

q.q: Writing and spreading a virus is mainly an offence under which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
o: Section 3
Section 1
Section 2
Section 3ZA
q.why: A virus impairs a computer or its data, which is an unauthorised act under section 3. Making it to supply to others is 3A.

q.q: Which best describes spyware?
o: Malware that attaches itself to files and copies itself into other files
Software that filters traffic entering and leaving a network using rules
Malware that secretly records a user's activity and sends it to someone else
A person who gets into a computer system without the owner's permission
q.why: Spyware secretly records activity such as keystrokes or websites visited and sends it on.

q.q: A criminal uses passwords captured by spyware to log in to a victim's bank account and transfer money. Which section best fits the log-in?
o: Section 3
Section 2
Section 3A
Section 3ZA
q.why: Using captured passwords to log in is section 1, or section 2 if the aim is fraud. Installing the spyware itself is section 3.

q.q: A penetration tester breaks into a company network with the company's written permission. Under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 this is...
o: not an offence, because the access was authorised
a section 1 offence, because the network was entered
a section 3 offence, because security was tested
an offence only if a weakness is actually found
q.why: Ethical hackers have written permission, so no offence is committed. Permission is the deciding factor.

q.q: Which laws replaced the Data Protection Act 1998?
o: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the UK GDPR
The UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018
The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 on its own
The Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: In 2018 the GDPR (now the UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018 replaced the 1998 Act. The 2025 Act amends them; it did not replace the 1998 Act.

q.q: What is personal data?
o: Any information that is stored on a person's own computer
Only a person's name, address and date of birth
Any information about a living person who can be identified from it
Any information about a person, living or dead
q.why: Personal data is any information about a living person who can be identified from it, including photos, email addresses, location data and IP addresses.

q.q: Which of these is special category data?
o: A pupil's postcode
A customer's email address
An employee's job title
A patient's medical condition
q.why: Health data is special category data because misuse could cause serious harm or discrimination.

q.q: When a GP practice stores patient records, who is the data subject?
o: The GP practice
The Information Commission
The patient
The IT company hosting the records
q.why: The data subject is the living person the data is about. The practice is the data controller.

q.q: A school uses a company to run its online dinner payments, and the company handles pupils' data for the school. What is that company's role?
o: Data controller
Data subject
Data Protection Officer
Data processor
q.why: A data processor handles data on the controller's behalf. The school decides why and how the data is used, so it is the controller.

q.q: What is the maximum fine for breaking UK data protection law?
o: £17.5 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is lower
£17.5 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher
£500,000 for any breach, however serious it is
4% of the organisation's UK profits for that year
q.why: Organisations can be fined up to £17.5 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

q.q: How many data protection principles does the UK GDPR have, compared with the 1998 Act?
o: Eight, compared with seven
Seven, compared with six
Eight, compared with ten
Seven, compared with eight
q.why: The UK GDPR has seven principles; the old 1998 Act had eight.

q.q: A youth club asks members for their political opinions although it has no need for them. Which principle is broken?
o: Data minimisation
Accuracy
Storage limitation
Purpose limitation
q.why: Data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is needed.

q.q: A firm keeps CVs from unsuccessful job applicants indefinitely. Which principle is broken?
o: Data minimisation
Storage limitation
Integrity and confidentiality
Accuracy
q.why: Personal data must not be kept longer than necessary.

q.q: A school passes parents' email addresses, collected for sending reports, to a holiday company. Which principle is broken?
o: Storage limitation
Purpose limitation
Accuracy
Accountability
q.why: Data collected for a stated purpose must not be reused for something unrelated.

q.q: Which principle requires the data controller to be able to prove it follows the other principles?
o: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
Integrity and confidentiality
Accountability
Purpose limitation
q.why: Accountability is new in the UK GDPR: the controller must be able to show it complies, for example with written policies and training records.

q.q: What happened to the 1998 Act's principle about transferring data outside the European Economic Area?
o: It was removed, so data can now be sent anywhere without any protection
It became the accuracy principle, so data sent abroad must be correct
It became a rule that data must not leave the UK without adequate protection
It became the accountability principle, so the controller must prove it
q.why: Overseas transfers are now covered by a rule that data must not be transferred outside the UK without adequate protection.

q.q: Which answer would earn the mark for 'State one data protection principle'?
o: Storage
Time
Data must be good
Personal data must not be kept for longer than necessary
q.why: Principles should be written in full; one-word answers such as 'time' or 'storage' rarely earn the mark.

q.q: A request to see a copy of the personal data an organisation holds about you is called...
o: a privacy notice
a data breach report
a right to rectification
a subject access request
q.why: A subject access request uses the right of access.

q.q: How long does an organisation normally have to answer a subject access request?
o: 72 hours
One month
14 days
One year
q.why: The normal deadline is one month. 72 hours is the deadline for reporting a breach to the regulator.

q.q: An organisation decides a subject access request is complex and extends the deadline as far as it is allowed. What is the longest total time it can take?
o: Two months
One month
Six months
Three months
q.why: The normal one month can be extended by up to two further months, giving three months in total.

q.q: A customer asks a gym to correct her wrongly spelt surname. Which right is she using?
o: Erasure
Rectification
Portability
Objection
q.why: Rectification is the right to have inaccurate or incomplete data corrected.

q.q: A customer asks an online shop to delete her old account and its data. Which right is she using?
o: Rectification
Restriction of processing
Erasure
Access
q.why: The right to erasure, or 'right to be forgotten', lets data be deleted in certain cases.

q.q: Which right of the data subject is absolute, meaning the organisation must always stop?
o: The right to have data erased
The right to data portability
The right to object to direct marketing
The right to restrict processing
q.why: Stopping data being used for direct marketing is an absolute right; erasure applies only in certain cases.

q.q: A loan application is refused automatically by a computer. Which right lets the applicant ask for a person to review the decision?
o: The right over automated decisions
The right to data portability
The right to rectification
The right to be informed
q.why: Data subjects need not be subject to some important decisions made purely by computer without safeguards such as a human review.

q.q: Which role must report a serious data breach to the regulator within 72 hours?
o: The data controller
The data subject
The Information Commission
The data processor
q.why: Reporting breaches likely to harm people is the data controller's legal duty.

q.q: A school discovers at 9am on Monday that a USB stick of pupils' medical notes has been lost, and the breach is likely to harm people. By when must it be reported to the Information Commission?
o: 9am on Tuesday
9am the following Monday
Within one month
9am on Thursday
q.why: Breaches likely to harm people must be reported within 72 hours (three days) of finding out: Monday 9am + 72 hours = Thursday 9am.

q.q: Why must a school have a Data Protection Officer?
o: Only schools with over 1000 pupils need one
The DPO replaces the school as data controller
The DPO writes the school's software
Schools are public bodies, which must appoint one
q.why: A DPO is required for public bodies such as schools and for organisations processing special category data on a large scale.

q.q: Which is a responsibility of the Data Protection Officer?
o: Deciding why and how the organisation processes data
Issuing fines to organisations that break the law
Keeping the UK register of fee-paying organisations
Advising staff, training them and monitoring compliance
q.why: The DPO advises, trains and monitors, and is the contact point for the regulator. Deciding purposes is the controller; fines and the register are the Information Commission.

q.q: Which of these is a responsibility of the Information Commission?
o: Issuing fines to organisations that break data protection law
Deciding what a school uses its pupils' data for
Writing each school's privacy notice for parents
Training a hospital's staff on data protection
q.why: The regulator enforces the law, including issuing enforcement notices and fines.

q.q: What is an enforcement notice?
o: A letter from a data subject asking to see a copy of their data
A form a data controller uses to report a breach to the regulator
An order from the regulator telling an organisation to change what it does
A notice explaining to customers how their data will be used
q.why: The regulator can order an organisation to change what it does by issuing an enforcement notice.

q.q: Which measure best keeps personal data accurate?
o: Encrypting laptops, USB drives and emails
Installing firewalls and anti-malware
Annual data-check sheets for families to confirm their details
Making regular backups of the database
q.why: Regular data checks keep records accurate and up to date. The others support security.

q.q: A school's office staff can see pupils' phone numbers but not their medical notes. Which measure is this?
o: Encryption
A retention policy
A privacy notice
Access rights
q.why: Access rights mean staff see only the data they need, supporting security and data minimisation.

q.q: A school asks parents for permission before posting pupils' photos online. Which principle does this support?
o: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
Storage limitation
Accuracy
Data minimisation
q.why: Consent forms and privacy notices mean people know what happens to their data, which supports lawfulness, fairness and transparency.

q.q: Which measure supports the storage limitation principle?
o: A retention policy with secure deletion or shredding
Annual data-check sheets sent to every family
Strong passwords and two-factor authentication
Staff training and an acceptable use policy
q.why: A retention policy destroys old records on schedule, so data is not kept longer than necessary.

q.q: Many data breaches are caused by human error, such as emailing the wrong person. Which measure best reduces this?
o: Firewalls and anti-malware software
Staff training and an acceptable use policy
Regular backups of all data
Annual data-check sheets
q.why: Staff training and an acceptable use policy reduce human error such as misdirected emails.

q.q: A website adds a pre-ticked £5 donation to every order. Which law is broken?
o: Computer Misuse Act 1990
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Data Protection Act 2018
Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: Pre-ticked boxes for extra payments are banned by the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013.

q.q: A council emails residents' home addresses to an estate agent without their knowledge. Which law is broken?
o: Computer Misuse Act 1990
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Data Protection Act 2018
Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: Mishandling personal data, here using it for an unrelated purpose, breaks data protection law.

q.q: A student downloads a paid video editor from a file-sharing site. Which law is broken?
o: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Data Protection Act 2018
Computer Misuse Act 1990
Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: Downloading paid software without permission is software piracy, a breach of copyright law.

q.q: A former employee uses an old password to log in to the company's system and delete files. Which law is broken?
o: Computer Misuse Act 1990
Data Protection Act 2018
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013
q.why: Getting into and interfering with a computer system without permission breaks the Computer Misuse Act 1990.

q.q: A hacker steals customers' personal data from a company that had no password protection on its database. Which statement is most accurate?
o: The hacker broke the Computer Misuse Act 1990 and the company may have broken data protection law
Only the company broke a law, because it failed to keep the data secure
Only the hacker broke a law, because the company was the victim
Both broke only the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
q.why: The hacker committed computer misuse; the company may also have broken data protection law by failing to keep the data secure. Say who broke which law.

q.q: When deciding which law has been broken in a scenario, what is the most useful question to ask first?
o: How much money was lost?
Was a computer used at all?
Which country is the website in?
What has been harmed?
q.why: Ask what was harmed: a purchase, creative work, a computer system or personal data. That points to the law.

q.q: Why might 'the CMA' lose the mark in a 'name the law' question?
o: CMA is the abbreviation for a different law about consumer rights
Examiners only accept the section number, not the name of the Act
The law has been replaced, so its name no longer earns any marks
Abbreviations and missing years can cost the mark; the full title is needed
q.why: Abbreviations such as 'CMA' or 'CDPA' and missing years can cost the mark; write out the full title and year.

q.q: Which statement about ethics is correct?
o: Anything that is legal must also be ethical
Ethics is about right and wrong, which can differ from what is legal
Ethics and the law always mean exactly the same
Ethics only applies to the actions of businesses
q.why: Some actions are legal but still wrong, such as personal browsing during paid work time.

q.q: A pupil repeatedly sends threatening messages to one classmate. What is this?
o: Trolling
Phishing
Cyberbullying
Hate speech
q.why: Cyberbullying repeatedly targets a particular person; trolling tries to provoke anyone.

q.q: Someone posts deliberately provocative comments under a news article to start arguments with strangers. What is this?
o: Trolling
Cyberbullying
Fake news
Oversharing
q.why: Trolling is deliberately posting provocative or offensive comments to upset people or start arguments. Mark schemes credit it separately from cyberbullying.

q.q: Why do employers have acceptable use policies?
o: To set rules on how staff may use the organisation's computers and internet
To give staff the right to install any software they like
To replace the need to follow data protection law
To make the organisation's network run faster
q.why: An acceptable use policy sets out what staff may and may not do with work ICT, for example to reduce personal browsing in work time.

q.q: A false story made to look like real news spreads quickly online and causes panic. What is this an example of?
o: Phishing
Fake news
Trolling
Plagiarism
q.why: Fake news is false or misleading stories made to look real and shared quickly; it misleads people and can stir up fear.

q.q: A teenager's profile shows her school, home town and live location to anyone. Which misuse risk is this?
o: Trolling
Hate speech
Oversharing
Piracy
q.why: Oversharing leaves personal details such as address, school or location public so strangers can find you.

q.q: Which of these is an ethical concern about GPS tracking?
o: Finding a lost phone
Being tracked without consent
Live bus arrival times
Better sat-nav directions
q.why: Tracking without consent invades privacy; the others are benefits.

q.q: How does a supermarket loyalty card collect data about customers?
o: It records where the customer parks their car
It reads the customer's fingerprints at the till
It scans the customer's emails for offers
It records what each customer buys and when
q.why: Loyalty cards record purchases so the shop can target adverts and offers.

q.q: What does GPS use to work out a device's position?
o: Signals from satellites orbiting the Earth
Signals from the nearest Wi-Fi router
Data stored on the device's SIM card
Cookies saved by the device's browser
q.why: GPS uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth to work out a device's exact position in real time.

q.q: Why might storing personal data on cloud servers in another country be a concern?
o: Data held abroad always loads more slowly
Servers abroad cannot have their data backed up
It always breaks the Computer Misuse Act 1990
Privacy laws there may be weaker than UK law
q.why: Cloud services may store data in other countries where privacy laws can be weaker than UK law.

q.q: Why can a geotagged photo posted on social media be a risk?
o: It can reveal where the person lives or goes to school
It makes the photo file too large to upload
It allows anyone to edit the original photo
It stops the photo being seen by friends
q.why: Geotagged photos reveal location, such as where someone lives or goes to school.

q.q: A bank closes branches as more customers use its app, so fewer counter staff are needed. What is this?
o: Job displacement
Upskilling
Teleworking
A change in work patterns
q.why: Job displacement is jobs being lost or changed because technology now does the work.

q.q: Which of these is a change in work patterns?
o: A new job as a game developer at a Belfast studio
Staff working from home three days a week using video calls
A robot replacing a welder on a factory line
A course for office staff on new spreadsheet software
q.why: Teleworking and hybrid working change how, when and where people work. The others are new jobs, displacement and upskilling.

q.q: Why do employers invest in upskilling their staff?
o: It reduces the number of computers that staff need to use
It keeps productivity up, improves morale and helps keep staff
It is required by the Computer Misuse Act 1990
It means the employer no longer has to pay wages
q.why: Good employers provide training because it keeps productivity up, improves morale and helps retention.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of teleworking for the employee?
o: Spending more time and money on commuting
Less flexibility to fit work around family
More traffic and pollution on the roads
Feeling isolated as home and work life blur
q.why: Teleworkers can feel isolated and find it harder to switch off. Saving on commuting and flexibility are advantages.

q.q: Why is poor rural broadband a disadvantage of teleworking in parts of Northern Ireland?
o: Rural broadband is not allowed to be used for work purposes
Staff need reliable broadband for cloud apps, remote access and video calls
Teleworking needs a separate cable from the office to each home
Teleworking only works in towns with a train station nearby
q.why: Teleworking relies on broadband, laptops, cloud apps, secure remote access and video calls, so poor rural broadband makes it harder.

q.q: Which health problem is mainly caused by repeating the same small movements, such as typing or clicking, for long periods?
o: Eye strain
Back strain
RSI
Hearing loss
q.why: Repetitive strain injury comes from repeated small movements, often with bent wrists.

q.q: An office worker gets headaches and blurred vision after hours at a screen. Which problem does this suggest?
o: RSI
Eye strain
Back strain
Carpal tunnel syndrome
q.why: Tired or sore eyes, headaches and blurred vision are symptoms of eye strain.

q.q: Which is a likely cause of back strain?
o: Glare and reflections on the screen
Typing with bent wrists for long periods
Sitting for long periods on an unsuitable chair
A screen that is set much too bright
q.why: Poor posture, an unsuitable chair and sitting still too long cause back strain. Glare and brightness cause eye strain; bent wrists cause RSI.

q.q: RSI can lead to which longer-term condition?
o: Blurred vision
Long-term mobility problems
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Headaches
q.why: RSI can lead to carpal tunnel syndrome. Long-term mobility problems are linked to back strain.

q.q: Which is a general workplace hazard in a computer room rather than a cause of RSI, back strain or eye strain?
o: Typing with bent wrists for long periods
Trailing cables, which are a trip hazard
Sitting still in a badly adjusted chair
A screen placed much too close to the eyes
q.why: Trailing cables are a trip hazard. The other options cause RSI, back strain and eye strain.

q.q: Which is an employer measure to reduce eye strain?
o: Providing anti-glare screens and free eye tests
Looking at something 20 feet away every 20 minutes
Adjusting the screen brightness when needed
Moving the screen to avoid glare from windows
q.why: Employers supply equipment and eye tests; the other options are things the employee does.

q.q: Which Northern Ireland law requires employers to assess computer workstations?
o: Health and Safety at Work (Northern Ireland) Order 1978
Computer Misuse Act 1990
Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations (Northern Ireland) 1992
Data Protection Act 2018
q.why: The DSE Regulations (NI) 1992 apply to regular screen users and require workstation assessments. The 1978 Order is the general health and safety law.

q.q: What type of fire extinguisher should be used on a computer fire?
o: CO₂
Water
Foam
A wet blanket
q.why: CO₂ does not conduct electricity and leaves no residue. Never use water on an electrical fire.

q.q: Under the DSE Regulations, what must employers do about eye tests for DSE users?
o: Provide free eye tests only for staff who already wear glasses outside work
Pay for all glasses that any employee needs, whatever they are used for
Provide free eye tests on request and pay for glasses needed specially for screen work
Provide eye tests only if a member of staff has made a compensation claim
q.why: Employers must provide free eye tests on request and pay for glasses if they are needed specially for screen work.

q.q: Which describes a correct position at an ideal workstation?
o: Top of the screen well above eye level, about half an arm's length away
Elbows bent at about 45°, with wrists angled upwards to the keyboard
Top of the screen at or just below eye level, about an arm's length away
Feet tucked under the chair, with the seat pressing behind the knees
q.why: The top of the screen should be at or just below eye level, about an arm's length away, with elbows at about 90° and wrists straight.

q.q: Which is an EMPLOYEE measure to reduce the risk of RSI?
o: Provide ergonomic keyboards and mice
Take regular breaks and keep wrists straight
Plan work so that it includes breaks
Provide adjustable chairs with lumbar support
q.why: Taking breaks and keeping wrists straight are employee measures; providing equipment and planning work are employer measures.
